title: Asynchronous token shaping and memory affinity notes
content:
Goal:
- Reduce 95th/99th latency spikes for long-tail conversational requests that trigger paged KV faults while keeping aggregate throughput high.

Context / motivation:
- We observe a class of requests with long historical context or bursty continuation patterns that cause repeated paged-KV loads. Those requests interleave short and long decode steps which confuses our current batching/prefetch heuristics and causes micro stalls in flash-attn kernels.
- Current approaches: coarse-grained prefetch windows (N tokens ahead), simple LRU page prefetch on first touch, and synchronous kernel ordering per request. Works well for steady streams but fails when token-length variance across lanes is high.

High-level idea: asynchronous token shaping + memory affinity steering
- Token shaping: split request stream into shaped micro-batches where each micro-batch groups tokens by expected KV-touch density and decode length estimate. Short-lifespan lanes are grouped separately from heavy-lifespan lanes.
- Asynchronous execution: allow shaped micro-batches to be scheduled out-of-order on device launch queues to keep tensor cores saturated while isolating stall-prone lanes.
- Memory affinity steering: place pages that are likely to be hot together in GPU memory slabs pinned to a launch stream; steer subsequent micro-batches that reuse the same pages to the same stream/SMs to improve locality and reduce page fault amplification.

Components and heuristics:
1) Per-request lightweight estimator (on CPU)
   - input: historical length, recent per-token KV touch ratio (ˆ), prompt type tag, model position bias
   - output: decode_length_estimate (int), kv_heft_score (0..1) where heft = expected new page faults per token
   - implementation: maintain short exponential moving averages per API token; fallback to model-profile defaults if insufficient history

2) Shaping micro-batches
   - sliding window over ready tokens (across requests)
   - candidate groups: 
       - "latency-critical short" (decode_length_estimate <= 8 AND kv_heft_score < 0.2)
       - "steady-medium" (8 < decode_length_estimate <= 64 or 0.2 <= kv_heft_score < 0.5)
       - "heavy-kv" (decode_length_estimate > 64 OR kv_heft_score >= 0.5)
   - aim: keep micro-batch size (in tokens) tuned per group; shorter for latency-critical, larger for heavy-kv to amortize prefetch costs.

3) Asynchronous GPU execution model
   - maintain multiple CUDA streams per GPU categorized by affinity slab (see below) and priority
   - launch policy: prefer to launch short-latency micro-batches on high-priority streams to minimize tail latency while scheduling heavy-kv work onto background streams that can be coalesced before execution
   - allow out-of-order completion: completion callbacks must rehydrate per-request state and update estimators

4) Memory affinity slabs and page placement
   - allocate pinned-device slabs (4–32MB) as logical hot regions mapped to stream groups. Pages from KV cache that are touched frequently are promoted to these slabs.
   - page promotion heuristics: counter-based promotion (touch count over sliding window), temporal decay, and cross-request reuse detection via small bloom filter per slab
   - eviction: per-slab LRU with soft thresholds to avoid global fragmentation; allow cross-slab migration during low GPU load windows

5) Kernel-level changes (FlashAttention/fused ops)
   - kernel registration: annotate fused kernels with expected KV-read sets (bitmap summary) so the runtime can prioritize launching kernels whose KV pages are already resident in targeted slabs
   - pre-kernel microprefetch hint: a tiny GPU-side prefetch kernel that touches page anchors in parallel (cooperative lanes) to avoid serial page faults inside heavy attention kernels
   - adaptive tile sizing: tune flash-attn tile sizes based on micro-batch group; heavy-kv tiles should prefer larger tiles to improve DMA throughput, short-latency tiles favor smaller tiles to reduce per-launch overhead

Microbench experiments (quick plan):
- Baselines: current sequential-stream scheduler with global LRU paged-KV and fixed prefetch window = 16 tokens.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 decode latency, GPU SM occupancy, page-fault rate per 10k tokens, throughput tokens/sec, tail waste (percentage of tokens stalled > 10ms)
- Sweep variables: micro-batch max tokens per group (2/8/32/128), number of affinity slabs (1/2/4/8), slab size (4/8/16/32MB), prefetch hint stride, tile size options for flash-attn kernels.
- Quick smoke tests on devbox (A40) + cluster sim (NVIDIA H100 cluster with paged memory simulated)

Pseudocode (shaper loop)
- while work_queue not empty:
    collect head tokens into candidate pool up to window_size W
    for each token t in pool:
       est = estimator(t.request_id)
       assign t to group = shape_bucket(est)
    for each group g in preferred_order([short, steady, heavy]):
       form microbatch M from oldest tokens in g up to group_size[g]
       pick stream S = pick_affinity_stream(M)
       launch_prefetch_hint(M, S)  // async lightweight prefetch kernel
       launch_fused_kernels(M, S)

Open questions / risks:
- Complexity of maintaining per-slab affinity vs fragmentation. Too many slabs can hurt generality and cause low slab utilization. Need telemetry to adapt slab count dynamically.
- Consistency when promoting/evicting pages concurrently with running kernels. Need safe handoff semantics to avoid use-after-free; possibly rely on reference counting or epoch-based reclamation.
- Estimator cold start: new requests may be misclassified leading to extra latency; mitigation: conservative defaults + fast online correction.
- Interactions with multi-tenant noise: background tenants may pollute slab locality; consider tenant-aware slabs for dedicated nodes.

Implementation milestones (rough):
- Week 0-2: add estimator skeleton and shaping loop in host-side scheduler (no affinity slabs) + unit tests
- Week 3-4: implement affinity streams and simple per-stream pinned slab allocator (read-only promotion path)
- Week 5-6: integrate prefetch hint kernel and kernel annotation hook for KV-bitmaps
- Week 7-8: run cluster experiments with production traces; iterate heuristics; add telemetry dashboards

Telemetry to collect:
- per-request kv_heft_score and final classification
- micro-batch composition distribution (tokens per group, requests per batch)
- slab hit rates and cross-slab migration counts
- prefetch hint success (fraction of hinted pages resident at kernel launch)
- kernel queueing latency by stream and micro-batch group

Quick notes / heuristics found in small experiments (devbox):
- Promoting pages with touch_count_threshold = 3 within 5s window reduced page-faults by ~45% for mid-size chats (32-128 tokens)
- Using 3 affinity slabs (short/steady/heavy) gave near-optimal packing on our traces; going to 8 slabs reduced slab hit rate due to fragmentation.
- Prefetch hint kernel with cooperative lane touch latency << issuing CPU-led prefetch commands (on our A40 test).

Next steps / action items:
- Ben: prototype estimator + shaping loop on host scheduler (WIP branch runtime/shaper).
- María: prototype slab allocator and simple promotion policy; add per-slab occupancy metrics.
- Ethan: add tiny prefetch hint kernel and microbench harness for tile-size sweeps.
- Schedule cross-team sync after initial smoke tests (in ~3 weeks).

Notes to reviewer:
- This is intentionally exploratory: focus review on feasibility concerns (safety for concurrent page ops) and whether the added scheduler complexity justifies expected tail improvements for our customer SLAs.
- If approved we'll iterate on a safety-first implementation (read-only promotion first) before enabling migration/eviction aggressions.

References / inspiration:
- prior internal notes on page-prefetch heuristics and slab-coordinator ideas
- external papers on asynchronous GPU execution and prefetching for irregular memory patterns
